title: Two Sum
statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to target. Each input has exactly one answer, and you may not use the same element twice. You can return the two indices in any order.
hint: For each number x, you need target - x. How can you check "have I seen target - x before?" in O(1)?
approach: Walk through the array once and keep a hash map from value to index. For each number x, look for target - x in the map. If it is there, we found the pair. If not, store x and move on. This works because every pair is found when we reach its second element, and the first element is already in the map. A brute force check of all pairs would take O(n^2).
solution: function twoSum(nums,target){const m=new Map();for(let i=0;i<nums.length;i++){const need=target-nums[i];if(m.has(need))return [m.get(need),i];m.set(nums[i],i);}return [];}
followups: What if the array is sorted? (Use two pointers with O(1) space.)
What if there can be many valid pairs and you must return all of them?

title: Group Anagrams
statement: Given an array of strings, group the words that are anagrams of each other. Return the groups in any order.
hint: Two words are anagrams if they have the same letters. Can you build a "key" from the letters that is the same for all anagrams?
approach: Anagrams become identical when their letters are sorted, so the sorted word works as a hash key. We put each word in a map under its key and return all the map values. Sorting a word of length k costs O(k log k). You can use a 26-count array as the key instead, which makes it O(k).
complexity: O(n * k log k) time, O(n * k) space (n words, max length k)
solution: function groupAnagrams(strs){const m=new Map();for(const s of strs){const k=s.split('').sort().join('');if(!m.has(k))m.set(k,[]);m.get(k).push(s);}return [...m.values()];}
followups: How would you do it in O(k) per word?
What if the words contain Unicode characters?

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: Given an unsorted array of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive numbers (like 1,2,3,4). The numbers do not need to be next to each other in the array. Your solution must run in O(n) time.
hint: Sorting is O(n log n). Put all numbers in a set. Which numbers are the START of a run?
approach: Put all numbers in a set. A number x starts a run only if x - 1 is not in the set. For each such start, count upward x+1, x+2, ... while they are in the set. Each number is visited at most twice (once in the outer loop, once while counting inside a single run), so the total is linear. Skipping non-starts is what prevents the O(n^2) behaviour.
solution: function longestConsecutive(nums){const s=new Set(nums);let best=0;for(const x of s){if(s.has(x-1))continue;let y=x;while(s.has(y+1))y++;best=Math.max(best,y-x+1);}return best;}
followups: How would you do this if the numbers arrive as a stream?

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k. The array can contain negative numbers and zeros.
hint: Use prefix sums. The sum of nums[i..j] is prefix[j] - prefix[i-1]. How many earlier prefixes equal prefix[j] - k?
approach: Keep a running prefix sum and a map counting how often each prefix sum has appeared (start with prefix 0 seen once). At each position, the number of subarrays ending here with sum k equals the count of earlier prefixes equal to (current - k). Add that to the answer, then record the current prefix. Sliding window does not work here because negative numbers break monotonicity, but prefix sums with a map always work.
solution: function subarraySum(nums,k){const m=new Map([[0,1]]);let sum=0,ans=0;for(const x of nums){sum+=x;ans+=m.get(sum-k)||0;m.set(sum,(m.get(sum)||0)+1);}return ans;}
followups: What if all numbers are positive? (A sliding window gives O(1) space.)

title: Valid Palindrome
statement: A phrase is a palindrome if, after making all letters lowercase and removing everything that is not a letter or digit, it reads the same forwards and backwards. Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome.
hint: Put one pointer at the start and one at the end. Skip characters that are not letters or digits.
approach: Use two pointers moving toward each other. Move the left pointer forward and the right pointer backward past any non-alphanumeric character. Then compare the two characters in lowercase. If they ever differ, the answer is false. If the pointers meet, it is a palindrome. This avoids building a cleaned copy, so extra space is O(1).

args: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama

solution: function isPalindrome(s){const ok=c=>/[a-z0-9]/i.test(c);let i=0,j=s.length-1;while(i<j){while(i<j&&!ok(s[i]))i++;while(i<j&&!ok(s[j]))j--;if(s[i].toLowerCase()!==s[j].toLowerCase())return false;i++;j--;}return true;}
followups: Valid Palindrome II: you may delete at most one character.

title: 3Sum
statement: Given an integer array nums, return all unique triplets [a, b, c] such that a + b + c = 0. The answer must not contain duplicate triplets.
hint: Sort the array. Fix the first number, then solve a sorted two-sum with two pointers. How do you skip duplicates?
approach: Sort the array. For each index i (skipping equal values), set left = i+1 and right = end. If the sum is too small move left up, if too large move right down. When the sum is 0, record the triplet and move both pointers past duplicate values. Sorting makes the two-pointer search valid and makes duplicates sit next to each other, so skipping them is easy.
complexity: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (excluding output and sort)
solution: function threeSum(nums){nums=[...nums].sort((a,b)=>a-b);const r=[];for(let i=0;i<nums.length-2;i++){if(i>0&&nums[i]===nums[i-1])continue;let l=i+1,h=nums.length-1;while(l<h){const s=nums[i]+nums[l]+nums[h];if(s<0)l++;else if(s>0)h--;else{r.push([nums[i],nums[l],nums[h]]);l++;h--;while(l<h&&nums[l]===nums[l-1])l++;while(l<h&&nums[h]===nums[h+1])h--;}}}return r;}
followups: 4Sum: how does the idea extend?
3Sum Closest.

title: Container With Most Water
statement: You are given an array height where height[i] is the height of a vertical line at position i. Pick two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container holding the most water. Return that maximum amount of water.
hint: Start with the widest container. Which line should you move to have any chance of a better answer?
approach: Start with pointers at both ends. The water is width * min(left height, right height). Move the pointer at the shorter line inward. Why: moving the taller line can never help, because the width shrinks and the height is still limited by the shorter line. Moving the shorter line might find a taller one. We check every candidate that could possibly be the best, in one pass.
solution: function maxArea(height){let l=0,r=height.length-1,best=0;while(l<r){best=Math.max(best,(r-l)*Math.min(height[l],height[r]));if(height[l]<height[r])l++;else r--;}return best;}
followups: Can you prove the greedy move never skips the best pair?

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: Given an array of non-negative integers representing an elevation map (each bar has width 1), compute how much rain water is trapped after it rains.
hint: Water above a bar = min(tallest bar to its left, tallest bar to its right) - its own height. Can you track those two maxima with two pointers?
approach: Keep two pointers and the running max from each side (leftMax, rightMax). The side with the smaller max decides the water level, because the other side already has something at least as tall. So if leftMax < rightMax, the bar at left holds leftMax - height[left] water (if positive), then move left. Otherwise do the same on the right. This is the O(1)-space version of the prefix-max / suffix-max arrays.
solution: function trap(height){let l=0,r=height.length-1,lm=0,rm=0,w=0;while(l<r){if(height[l]<height[r]){lm=Math.max(lm,height[l]);w+=lm-height[l];l++;}else{rm=Math.max(rm,height[r]);w+=rm-height[r];r--;}}return w;}
followups: Solve it with a monotonic stack instead.
What about the 2-D version (Trapping Rain Water II)?

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring that has no repeated characters.
hint: Keep a window [left, right]. When a character repeats, how far should left move?
approach: Move right across the string and remember the last index where each character appeared. If the current character was seen inside the window, jump left to just after that earlier position. The window always has unique characters, and we record its size at each step. Each index is visited once, so it is linear.
solution: function lengthOfLongestSubstring(s){const last=new Map();let l=0,best=0;for(let r=0;r<s.length;r++){if(last.has(s[r])&&last.get(s[r])>=l)l=last.get(s[r])+1;last.set(s[r],r);best=Math.max(best,r-l+1);}return best;}
followups: At most k distinct characters.

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement: You are given an uppercase string s and an integer k. You may change at most k characters to any other letter. Return the length of the longest substring that can become all the same letter.
hint: A window is valid if (window size - count of its most common letter) <= k.
approach: Slide a window and count letters in it. The window can be fixed to one letter if the characters that are not the most common one are at most k. So we need size - maxCount <= k. When it breaks, shrink from the left by one. We never need to lower maxCount when shrinking: the window only grows when a new larger maxCount appears, and that is the only case where the answer can improve.
solution: function characterReplacement(s,k){const cnt={};let l=0,mx=0,best=0;for(let r=0;r<s.length;r++){cnt[s[r]]=(cnt[s[r]]||0)+1;mx=Math.max(mx,cnt[s[r]]);if(r-l+1-mx>k){cnt[s[l]]--;l++;}best=Math.max(best,r-l+1);}return best;}
followups: Why is it safe not to decrease maxCount when the window shrinks?

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement: Given strings s and t, return the smallest substring of s that contains every character of t (with the right counts). If there is none, return an empty string.
hint: Expand right until the window is valid, then shrink left as much as possible. Track how many required characters are still missing.
approach: Count the needed letters from t. Move right and decrease the need count; keep a "missing" counter of how many required characters are still not covered. When missing hits 0 the window is valid: try to shrink from the left while it stays valid, and record the smallest window. Each pointer moves only forward, so total work is linear.
solution: function minWindow(s,t){const need={};for(const c of t)need[c]=(need[c]||0)+1;let missing=t.length,l=0,bs=-1,bl=Infinity;for(let r=0;r<s.length;r++){if(need[s[r]]>0)missing--;need[s[r]]=(need[s[r]]||0)-1;if(missing===0){while(need[s[l]]<0){need[s[l]]++;l++;}if(r-l+1<bl){bl=r-l+1;bs=l;}need[s[l]]++;missing++;l++;}}return bs<0?'':s.substr(bs,bl);}
followups: What if s is a huge stream and cannot be stored?

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: Given an array nums and a window size k, the window moves from left to right one step at a time. Return an array with the maximum value of each window.
hint: Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. The front is always the maximum.
approach: Maintain a deque of indices with decreasing values. For each new index i: pop from the back while the value there is <= nums[i] (they can never be a maximum again), push i, and pop from the front if it is outside the window. Once the first window is complete, nums[front] is the answer for that window. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the cost is amortized O(1) per element.
solution: function maxSlidingWindow(nums,k){const dq=[];let head=0;const res=[];for(let i=0;i<nums.length;i++){while(dq.length>head&&nums[dq[dq.length-1]]<=nums[i])dq.pop();dq.push(i);if(dq[head]<=i-k)head++;if(i>=k-1)res.push(nums[dq[head]]);}return res;}
followups: Solve it with a heap and compare the complexity.

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string containing only the characters ()[]{}, return true if every opening bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, in the correct order.
hint: The most recent opening bracket must be closed first. Which data structure gives you "most recent first"?
approach: Use a stack. Push each opening bracket. For a closing bracket, the top of the stack must be its matching opener; pop it. If the stack is empty or the types differ, return false. At the end the stack must be empty. The stack works because brackets nest: the last opened is always the first to close.
solution: function isValid(s){const m={')':'(',']':'[','}':'{'};const st=[];for(const c of s){if(m[c]){if(st.pop()!==m[c])return false;}else st.push(c);}return st.length===0;}
followups: Return the minimum number of insertions to make it valid.

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: Given an array temperatures, return an array answer where answer[i] is the number of days you must wait after day i to get a warmer temperature. If there is no warmer day, answer[i] is 0.
hint: You want the next greater element to the right. Keep a stack of days still waiting for a warmer day.
approach: Use a monotonic stack of indices whose temperatures are decreasing. For each day i, while the top of the stack has a lower temperature than today, pop it and set its answer to i - top. Then push i. Every index is pushed once and popped once, so the total is linear. The stack stays decreasing because anything colder than the new day is removed first.
solution: function dailyTemperatures(temperatures){const res=new Array(temperatures.length).fill(0),st=[];for(let i=0;i<temperatures.length;i++){while(st.length&&temperatures[st[st.length-1]]<temperatures[i]){const j=st.pop();res[j]=i-j;}st.push(i);}return res;}
followups: Next Greater Element II (circular array).

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: Given an array heights of bar heights in a histogram (each bar has width 1), return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the histogram.
hint: For each bar, how far can a rectangle with that bar's height extend left and right? A monotonic stack finds the first shorter bar on each side.
approach: Keep a stack of indices with increasing heights. When a bar is lower than the top, the top bar cannot extend further right, so pop it. Its height is the rectangle height; its width goes from the new stack top + 1 to the current index - 1. Add a sentinel 0 bar at the end to flush the stack. Each bar enters and leaves the stack once.
solution: function largestRectangleArea(heights){const h=[...heights,0],st=[];let best=0;for(let i=0;i<h.length;i++){while(st.length&&h[st[st.length-1]]>=h[i]){const top=h[st.pop()];const left=st.length?st[st.length-1]:-1;best=Math.max(best,top*(i-left-1));}st.push(i);}return best;}
followups: Maximal Rectangle in a binary matrix builds on this problem.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement: Evaluate an arithmetic expression given in Reverse Polish Notation as an array of tokens. Valid operators are +, -, * and /. Division truncates toward zero. The expression is always valid.
hint: When you see an operator, its two operands are the two most recent values.
approach: Scan the tokens. Numbers are pushed on a stack. For an operator, pop the right operand and then the left operand, compute, and push the result. In the end the stack holds one value, the answer. Division must truncate toward zero, so use Math.trunc.
solution: function evalRPN(tokens){const st=[];for(const t of tokens){if('+-*/'.includes(t)&&t.length===1){const b=st.pop(),a=st.pop();st.push(t==='+'?a+b:t==='-'?a-b:t==='*'?a*b:Math.trunc(a/b));}else st.push(Number(t));}return st[0];}
followups: Convert an infix expression with parentheses to RPN (shunting-yard).

title: Binary Search
statement: Given a sorted array of distinct integers nums and a target, return the index of target, or -1 if it is not in the array. Your solution must run in O(log n).
hint: Compare target with the middle element. Which half can you throw away?
approach: Keep a range [lo, hi]. Look at the middle. If it equals target, return it. If target is larger, the answer can only be on the right, so lo = mid + 1; otherwise hi = mid - 1. The range halves each step, so there are about log2(n) steps. Compute mid as lo + floor((hi - lo) / 2) in languages with overflow.
solution: function search(nums,target){let lo=0,hi=nums.length-1;while(lo<=hi){const mid=lo+((hi-lo)>>1);if(nums[mid]===target)return mid;if(nums[mid]<target)lo=mid+1;else hi=mid-1;}return -1;}
followups: Return the first index where target could be inserted (lower bound).

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated at some unknown pivot (for example [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] became [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]). Given the rotated array and a target, return its index or -1. Run in O(log n).
hint: At any middle point, at least one half is properly sorted. Check whether the target lies inside that sorted half.
approach: Do a binary search. At mid, if nums[lo] <= nums[mid] then the left half is sorted. If the target lies between nums[lo] and nums[mid], go left; otherwise go right. If instead the right half is sorted, do the mirror check. In every step we can say for sure which half to discard, so it stays logarithmic.
solution: function searchRotated(nums,target){let lo=0,hi=nums.length-1;while(lo<=hi){const m=(lo+hi)>>1;if(nums[m]===target)return m;if(nums[lo]<=nums[m]){if(nums[lo]<=target&&target<nums[m])hi=m-1;else lo=m+1;}else{if(nums[m]<target&&target<=nums[hi])lo=m+1;else hi=m-1;}}return -1;}
followups: What if the array may contain duplicates? How does the worst case change?

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: A sorted array of distinct integers was rotated between 1 and n times. Return its minimum element in O(log n) time.
hint: Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If mid is bigger, where must the minimum be?
approach: Binary search on the rotation point. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop (and the minimum) is to the right of mid, so lo = mid + 1. Otherwise the minimum is at mid or to its left, so hi = mid. When lo meets hi we stand on the minimum. Comparing with hi (not lo) avoids trouble when the array is not rotated.
solution: function findMin(nums){let lo=0,hi=nums.length-1;while(lo<hi){const m=(lo+hi)>>1;if(nums[m]>nums[hi])lo=m+1;else hi=m;}return nums[lo];}
followups: Handle duplicates (Find Minimum II).

title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: Koko has piles of bananas, piles[i] in the i-th pile, and h hours. Each hour she picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it (if the pile has fewer, she finishes it and waits). Return the smallest integer k that lets her eat all bananas within h hours.
hint: If speed k works, then any faster speed works too. That is a monotonic yes/no, so you can binary search on k.
approach: The answer lies between 1 and the biggest pile. For a given k, the hours needed is the sum of ceil(pile / k). This is non-increasing as k grows, so binary search for the smallest k whose hours <= h. This "binary search on the answer" pattern works whenever feasibility is monotonic and checking one candidate is cheap.
complexity: O(n log M) time (M = max pile), O(1) space
solution: function minEatingSpeed(piles,h){let lo=1,hi=Math.max(...piles);while(lo<hi){const k=(lo+hi)>>1;let t=0;for(const p of piles)t+=Math.ceil(p/k);if(t<=h)hi=k;else lo=k+1;}return lo;}
followups: Same idea: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days, Split Array Largest Sum.

title: Reverse Linked List
statement: The head of a singly linked list is given as an array of values (for example [1,2,3] means 1 -> 2 -> 3). Reverse the list and return it as an array.
hint: Walk through the list and flip each next pointer to point at the previous node. Keep track of prev, cur and the saved next.
approach: Keep three things: prev (starts null), cur (starts at head) and next. For each node, save cur.next, point cur.next to prev, then move prev and cur one step forward. When cur becomes null, prev is the new head. Each pointer is changed once, so it is linear time and needs no extra memory. In the array form, this is the same as reversing the array, but practise the pointer version.
followups: Reverse it recursively.
Reverse only the nodes between positions left and right.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: Two sorted linked lists are given as arrays list1 and list2. Merge them into one sorted list and return it as an array.
hint: Use a dummy head node. Always attach the smaller of the two current nodes.
approach: Create a dummy node and a tail pointer. While both lists have nodes, link the smaller node to the tail and advance that list. When one list ends, link the rest of the other (it is already sorted). The dummy node removes the special case of an empty result. We touch each node once.
complexity: O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space
followups: Merge k sorted lists.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
statement: Given a linked list as an array and an integer n, remove the n-th node from the END of the list and return the list as an array. Try to do it in one pass.
hint: Use two pointers with a gap of n nodes between them.
approach: Add a dummy node before the head. Move a fast pointer n steps ahead. Then move fast and slow together until fast reaches the last node. Now slow sits just before the node to delete, so set slow.next = slow.next.next. The gap of n nodes means slow lands exactly where we need. The dummy node handles removing the head.
followups: Find the middle node using the same fast/slow idea.

title: Add Two Numbers
statement: Two non-negative numbers are stored as linked lists (given as arrays) with the digits in REVERSE order, so [2,4,3] means 342. Add the two numbers and return the sum in the same format as an array.
hint: It is school addition: add digit by digit and carry. Do not forget a final carry.
approach: Walk both lists together. At each step, sum = digit1 + digit2 + carry. The new digit is sum % 10 and the new carry is floor(sum / 10). Treat a finished list as digit 0 and continue until both lists and the carry are all finished. Because the digits are stored least significant first, we can add in a single forward pass.
complexity: O(max(n, m)) time, O(1) extra space
followups: What if the digits are stored in normal order (Add Two Numbers II)?

title: Linked List Cycle
statement: A linked list is given as an array head. The number pos tells which index the LAST node's next pointer connects to (-1 means no cycle). Return true if the list has a cycle. Try to use O(1) extra space.
hint: Use two pointers moving at different speeds. If there is a loop, the fast one will catch the slow one.
approach: Floyd's tortoise and hare: slow moves one step, fast moves two. If there is no cycle, fast reaches the end (null). If there is a cycle, both stay in the loop forever and fast gains one step per round on slow, so they must meet. A hash set of visited nodes also works but costs O(n) memory. Here we build the list and connect the tail to node pos to create the cycle.
followups: Find the node where the cycle begins (Linked List Cycle II).

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: A binary tree is given as a level-order array where null means a missing child (for example [3,9,20,null,null,15,7]). Return its maximum depth, the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.
hint: The depth of a tree is 1 + the larger depth of its two subtrees.
approach: Use recursion (DFS): an empty tree has depth 0; otherwise depth = 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). Each node is visited once. A BFS that counts the number of levels also works and avoids deep recursion on very skewed trees. A helper that builds nodes from the level-order array is included in the solution.
complexity: O(n) time, O(h) space (h = tree height)
followups: Do it iteratively with BFS.
Minimum depth of a binary tree.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: Given a binary tree as a level-order array with null for missing children, return its values level by level, from left to right, as a list of lists.
hint: Use a queue. At each round, process exactly the nodes that are in the queue right now.
approach: BFS with a queue. Before each round, read the queue size: those nodes make up one level. Pop them one by one, record their values and push their children. Repeating this gives one list per level. Each node is queued once.
complexity: O(n) time, O(w) space (w = widest level)
followups: Zigzag level order traversal.
Right side view of the tree.

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: Given a binary tree as a level-order array, return true if it is a valid BST: for every node, all values in its left subtree are smaller and all values in its right subtree are larger (no equal values allowed).
hint: Checking only a node and its direct children is not enough. Pass down the allowed range (low, high) to each node.
approach: Do a DFS and carry a range. The root can be anything. Going left, the upper bound becomes the parent value; going right, the lower bound becomes the parent value. A node is invalid if its value is not strictly between low and high. This catches the case where a deep node breaks a rule set by a far ancestor. An in-order traversal must also be strictly increasing, which is an equal approach.
followups: Find the k-th smallest element in a BST.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
statement: Given a binary tree as a level-order array and the values p and q of two nodes that exist in the tree (all values are unique), return the value of their lowest common ancestor. A node can be an ancestor of itself.
hint: Search both subtrees. What does it mean if p is found on the left and q on the right?
approach: Recursive DFS: if the current node is null, p or q, return it. Otherwise search left and right. If both sides return something, the current node is where p and q split, so it is the LCA. If only one side returns something, pass it up. Because we return the node itself when it equals p or q, the case "p is an ancestor of q" also works.
followups: How is it simpler if the tree is a BST?
What if p or q might not exist?

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement: A path in a binary tree is any sequence of connected nodes where each node appears at most once; it does not need to pass through the root. Given the tree as a level-order array (values can be negative), return the maximum sum of any path.
hint: For each node, compute the best path that goes down from it into one side. Then combine two sides at that node.
approach: DFS returns, for each node, the best "downward" path sum starting at that node: node.val + max(0, best left, best right) with negative branches ignored. While at the node, the best path that bends here is node.val + max(0, left) + max(0, right); update a global answer with it. The returned value can only use one side because a parent cannot use a path that splits.
followups: Return the path itself, not only its sum.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k-th largest element in sorted order (not the k-th distinct element).
hint: Keep only the k biggest numbers seen so far. Which heap makes the smallest of them easy to remove?
approach: Use a min-heap of size k. Push each number; if the heap grows beyond k, pop the smallest. After all numbers, the heap holds the k largest and its top is the k-th largest. A heap push or pop costs O(log k), so the total is O(n log k), better than sorting when k is small. Quickselect gives O(n) average time.
complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
followups: Solve it in O(n) average time with quickselect.
How would you do it for a stream of numbers?

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. The answer is guaranteed to be unique. You can return them in any order.
hint: First count frequencies. Then you need the k biggest counts. A size-k min-heap works.
approach: Count each number with a hash map. Then push (count, value) pairs into a min-heap ordered by count, and pop whenever the heap has more than k items. What remains are the k most frequent. This is O(n log k). Bucket sort by frequency (index = count) gives O(n) because counts never exceed n.
complexity: O(n log k) time, O(n) space
followups: Solve it in O(n) with bucket sort.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
statement: You are given k sorted lists (each given as an array). Merge them into one sorted list and return it as an array.
hint: At every step you need the smallest of the k current heads. A min-heap gives that in O(log k).
approach: Put the first element of every non-empty list into a min-heap as (value, list index, position). Pop the smallest, add it to the result, and push the next element from the same list. Each of the N total elements is pushed and popped once at O(log k), so the cost is O(N log k). Merging lists one after another would be O(N * k).
complexity: O(N log k) time, O(k) space
followups: Merge using divide and conquer instead of a heap.

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement: Design a MedianFinder with addNum(num) and findMedian(). The input is a list of operation names and a list of argument lists. Return a list with the result of each operation: null for the constructor and addNum, and the current median for findMedian.
hint: Split the numbers into a smaller half and a larger half. Which heap should hold each half?
approach: Keep a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, sized so the max-heap has the same count or one more. On add: push into the max-heap, move its top to the min-heap, and if the min-heap is bigger, move its top back. The median is the max-heap top (odd count) or the average of the two tops (even count). Add is O(log n), find is O(1).
complexity: addNum O(log n), findMedian O(1), O(n) space
followups: What if all numbers are between 0 and 100?
What if 99% of numbers are in that range?

title: Merge Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals [start, end], merge all overlapping intervals and return the non-overlapping intervals that cover the same ranges, sorted by start. Intervals that touch (like [1,4] and [4,5]) are merged.
hint: Sort by start. Then each interval either overlaps the last merged one or starts a new one.
approach: Sort intervals by start. Keep an output list. For each interval, if its start is <= the end of the last output interval, they overlap, so extend the last end to max(last end, this end). Otherwise push it as new. After sorting, only the most recent merged interval can overlap the next one, which is why one pass is enough.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
solution: function merge(intervals){const a=[...intervals].sort((x,y)=>x[0]-y[0]);const r=[];for(const [s,e] of a){if(r.length&&s<=r[r.length-1][1])r[r.length-1][1]=Math.max(r[r.length-1][1],e);else r.push([s,e]);}return r;}
followups: Insert Interval when the list is already sorted, in O(n).

title: Insert Interval
statement: You get a sorted list of non-overlapping intervals and one new interval. Insert the new interval so the list stays sorted and non-overlapping, merging if needed. Return the new list.
hint: There are three groups: intervals fully before the new one, intervals that overlap it, and intervals fully after.
approach: Scan once. Copy all intervals that end before the new one starts. For intervals that overlap (their start <= new end), absorb them: new start = min of starts, new end = max of ends. Add the merged interval, then copy the rest. No sorting is needed because the input is already sorted, so it is linear.
solution: function insert(intervals,newInterval){const r=[];let [s,e]=newInterval,i=0;const n=intervals.length;while(i<n&&intervals[i][1]<s)r.push(intervals[i++]);while(i<n&&intervals[i][0]<=e){s=Math.min(s,intervals[i][0]);e=Math.max(e,intervals[i][1]);i++;}r.push([s,e]);while(i<n)r.push(intervals[i++]);return r;}
followups: Do it with binary search to find the position first.

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement: Given an array of intervals, return the minimum number of intervals you must remove so that the remaining ones do not overlap. Intervals that only touch ([1,2] and [2,3]) do not overlap.
hint: Think of choosing the maximum number of intervals to KEEP. Which interval should you pick first?
approach: Greedy: sort by end time. Keep the interval that ends earliest, since it leaves the most room for the rest. Then for each next interval: if it starts at or after the end of the last kept one, keep it; otherwise remove it. The answer is the number removed. Choosing the earliest end can never be worse than any other choice, which is the exchange argument.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
solution: function eraseOverlapIntervals(intervals){const a=[...intervals].sort((x,y)=>x[1]-y[1]);let end=-Infinity,rem=0;for(const [s,e] of a){if(s>=end)end=e;else rem++;}return rem;}
followups: Minimum number of arrows to burst balloons is the same idea.

title: Meeting Rooms II
statement: Given an array of meeting time intervals [start, end], return the minimum number of meeting rooms needed so that no two meetings overlap in the same room. A meeting ending at time t and another starting at t can share a room.
hint: Think of a timeline. How many meetings are running at the busiest moment?
approach: Sort all start times and all end times separately. Sweep with two pointers: if the next event is a start (start < current end), we need one more room; otherwise a meeting ended, so a room is freed. The most rooms in use at any time is the answer. A min-heap of end times also works: reuse the room of the earliest finishing meeting if it is free.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
solution: function minMeetingRooms(intervals){const s=intervals.map(x=>x[0]).sort((a,b)=>a-b),e=intervals.map(x=>x[1]).sort((a,b)=>a-b);let rooms=0,best=0,j=0;for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++){if(s[i]<e[j])rooms++;else j++;best=Math.max(best,rooms);}return best;}
followups: Also return which room each meeting uses.

title: Jump Game
statement: You start at index 0 of an array nums. Each nums[i] is the maximum jump length from position i. Return true if you can reach the last index.
hint: Track the farthest index you can reach so far. If you are ever standing beyond that, you are stuck.
approach: Scan left to right and keep far = the farthest reachable index. At index i, if i > far we cannot even get here, so return false. Otherwise update far = max(far, i + nums[i]). If far reaches the last index we are done. It works because reachability is "closed": if you can reach index j, you can reach everything before j.
solution: function canJump(nums){let far=0;for(let i=0;i<nums.length;i++){if(i>far)return false;far=Math.max(far,i+nums[i]);}return true;}
followups: A DP solution is O(n^2). Why is greedy correct?

title: Jump Game II
statement: Same setup as Jump Game, but the last index is always reachable. Return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index.
hint: Think in BFS levels: all indices reachable with j jumps form a range. How far does the next range reach?
approach: Treat it as BFS on ranges. Keep curEnd (the farthest index reachable with the current number of jumps) and farthest (the farthest reachable with one more jump). Scan indices; update farthest. When you pass curEnd, you must take another jump, so jumps++ and curEnd = farthest. Stop before the last index. Each index is scanned once.
solution: function jump(nums){let jumps=0,end=0,far=0;for(let i=0;i<nums.length-1;i++){far=Math.max(far,i+nums[i]);if(i===end){jumps++;end=far;}}return jumps;}
followups: Prove why the greedy range expansion gives the minimum.

title: Gas Station
statement: There are stations on a circle. gas[i] is the fuel at station i and cost[i] is the fuel needed to drive to the next station. You start with an empty tank. Return the index of the station from which you can complete the full circle, or -1 if it is impossible. The answer is unique if it exists.
hint: If the total gas is less than the total cost, it is impossible. If you run out starting at station s, can any station between s and the failure point be a good start?
approach: If sum(gas) < sum(cost) the answer is -1. Otherwise a solution exists. Scan once keeping the current tank. If the tank goes negative at station i, no station from the current start up to i can work (each had a non-negative tank when reaching i, so starting later only has less fuel), so set the start to i + 1 and reset the tank. The final start is the answer.
solution: function canCompleteCircuit(gas,cost){let total=0,tank=0,start=0;for(let i=0;i<gas.length;i++){const d=gas[i]-cost[i];total+=d;tank+=d;if(tank<0){start=i+1;tank=0;}}return total>=0?start:-1;}
followups: What if several starting stations are valid?

title: Partition Labels
statement: Split a string s into as many parts as possible so that each letter appears in at most one part. Return a list with the size of each part.
hint: For each letter, find its last position. A part must at least reach the last position of every letter inside it.
approach: First record the last index of each letter. Then scan the string: keep the current part end = max of last[c] for letters seen so far in this part. When the index i equals that end, no letter inside the part appears later, so cut here and record the size. Cutting as soon as possible gives the most parts.
solution: function partitionLabels(s){const last={};for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++)last[s[i]]=i;const res=[];let start=0,end=0;for(let i=0;i<s.length;i++){end=Math.max(end,last[s[i]]);if(i===end){res.push(end-start+1);start=i+1;}}return res;}
followups: How is this like merging intervals?

title: Subsets
statement: Given an array of distinct integers nums, return all possible subsets (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets. You can return the subsets in any order.
hint: For each number you have two choices: take it or skip it.
approach: Use backtracking. Keep a current path. At each index i, add the current path to the answer, then for each j >= i push nums[j], recurse with j + 1, and pop it. Moving the start index forward means each subset is built in one fixed order, so there are no duplicates. There are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to n.
complexity: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) recursion space (plus output)
solution: function subsets(nums){const res=[],path=[];const go=i=>{res.push([...path]);for(let j=i;j<nums.length;j++){path.push(nums[j]);go(j+1);path.pop();}};go(0);return res;}
followups: Subsets II: the input may contain duplicates.
Do it iteratively with bitmasks.

title: Permutations
statement: Given an array of distinct integers, return all its permutations. To make answers easy to compare, build them in this order: at each position try the unused numbers from left to right (index order).
hint: Keep a used[] flag per index. At each depth, choose any unused element.
approach: Backtracking: path holds the chosen numbers. When the path has n numbers, save a copy. Otherwise loop over all indexes; if not used, mark it used, push it, recurse, then undo both. Undoing the choice after the recursive call is the key backtracking step. There are n! permutations, each copied in O(n).
complexity: O(n * n!) time, O(n) extra space
solution: function permute(nums){const res=[],path=[],used=new Array(nums.length).fill(false);const go=()=>{if(path.length===nums.length){res.push([...path]);return;}for(let i=0;i<nums.length;i++){if(used[i])continue;used[i]=true;path.push(nums[i]);go();path.pop();used[i]=false;}};go();return res;}
followups: Permutations II with duplicate numbers.
Next Permutation without recursion.

title: Combination Sum
statement: Given an array of distinct positive integers candidates and a target, return all unique combinations that add up to target. You may use the same number any number of times. Combinations that differ only in order count as the same. Any order of the output is fine.
hint: To avoid duplicates, only move forward in the candidate list: never go back to a smaller index.
approach: Backtracking with a start index. At each step try candidates from start to the end. Add a candidate, recurse with the same index (because reuse is allowed) and the smaller remaining target, then remove it. Stop when the remaining target is 0 (save) or negative (prune). Sorting the candidates lets you stop the loop early once a number is too big.
complexity: O(N^(T/M)) time in the worst case (T = target, M = smallest candidate), O(T/M) space
solution: function combinationSum(candidates,target){const res=[],path=[];const go=(i,rem)=>{if(rem===0){res.push([...path]);return;}for(let j=i;j<candidates.length;j++){if(candidates[j]>rem)continue;path.push(candidates[j]);go(j,rem-candidates[j]);path.pop();}};go(0,target);return res;}
followups: Combination Sum II: each number can be used once and the input has duplicates.

title: Word Search
statement: You get a grid of letters (an array of equal-length strings) and a word. Return true if the word can be built by moving to horizontally or vertically adjacent cells, without using the same cell twice in one word.
hint: Start a DFS from each cell that matches the first letter. Mark cells you are using, and unmark them when you go back.
approach: For every cell, run DFS(r, c, k) that checks if the k-th letter matches. Mark the cell as visited (for example by replacing it with a special character), try the four neighbours for letter k + 1, then restore the cell. The restore step is the backtracking part: another start may use that cell. The worst case explores 4 (really 3) branches per letter.
complexity: O(m * n * 3^L) time, O(L) space (L = word length)
solution: function exist(board,word){const g=board.map(r=>r.split(''));const R=g.length,C=g[0].length;const go=(r,c,k)=>{if(k===word.length)return true;if(r<0||c<0||r>=R||c>=C||g[r][c]!==word[k])return false;const t=g[r][c];g[r][c]='#';const ok=go(r+1,c,k+1)||go(r-1,c,k+1)||go(r,c+1,k+1)||go(r,c-1,k+1);g[r][c]=t;return ok;};for(let r=0;r<R;r++)for(let c=0;c<C;c++)if(go(r,c,0))return true;return false;}
followups: Word Search II: many words at once (use a trie).

title: N-Queens II
statement: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other (same row, column or diagonal). Return the number of distinct solutions.
hint: Place one queen per row. Which columns and diagonals are already taken?
approach: Backtrack row by row. For each row try each column that is not in a used column, and whose two diagonals (row - col and row + col) are free. Keep three sets (or bitmasks) for columns and the two diagonal directions, add them when placing, remove them when going back. Pruning attacked squares early cuts the search from n^n to a much smaller tree.
solution: function totalNQueens(n){const cols=new Set(),d1=new Set(),d2=new Set();const go=r=>{if(r===n)return 1;let c=0;for(let j=0;j<n;j++){if(cols.has(j)||d1.has(r-j)||d2.has(r+j))continue;cols.add(j);d1.add(r-j);d2.add(r+j);c+=go(r+1);cols.delete(j);d1.delete(r-j);d2.delete(r+j);}return c;};return go(0);}
followups: Speed it up with bitmasks.
Return the actual boards (N-Queens).

title: Number of Islands
statement: Given a grid as an array of strings of "1" (land) and "0" (water), return the number of islands. An island is a group of land cells connected horizontally or vertically.
hint: When you find an unvisited land cell, count one island and then flood-fill everything connected to it.
approach: Scan every cell. When a "1" is found, increment the count and run DFS/BFS that turns all connected land cells into "0" (marking them visited). Because each island is erased the first time we meet it, it is counted exactly once. Each cell is processed a constant number of times.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space worst case for recursion
solution: function numIslands(grid){if(!grid.length)return 0;const g=grid.map(r=>r.split(''));const R=g.length,C=g[0].length;let n=0;const fill=(r,c)=>{const st=[[r,c]];g[r][c]='0';while(st.length){const [a,b]=st.pop();for(const [x,y] of [[a+1,b],[a-1,b],[a,b+1],[a,b-1]])if(x>=0&&y>=0&&x<R&&y<C&&g[x][y]==='1'){g[x][y]='0';st.push([x,y]);}}};for(let r=0;r<R;r++)for(let c=0;c<C;c++)if(g[r][c]==='1'){n++;fill(r,c);}return n;}
followups: Count islands while land cells are added one at a time (Number of Islands II, union-find).

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: A grid has 0 (empty), 1 (fresh orange) and 2 (rotten orange). Every minute, each fresh orange next to a rotten one (up, down, left, right) becomes rotten. Return the minimum number of minutes until no fresh orange is left, or -1 if it is impossible.
hint: All rotten oranges start spreading at the same time. This is a BFS with many starting points.
approach: Do a multi-source BFS. Put all rotten oranges in the queue first and count the fresh ones. Process the queue level by level; each level is one minute. When a neighbour is fresh, make it rotten, decrease the fresh count and queue it. At the end the answer is the number of levels used if fresh == 0, else -1. BFS gives the earliest time every orange rots.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
solution: function orangesRotting(grid){const g=grid.map(r=>[...r]);const R=g.length,C=g[0].length;let q=[],fresh=0;for(let r=0;r<R;r++)for(let c=0;c<C;c++){if(g[r][c]===2)q.push([r,c]);else if(g[r][c]===1)fresh++;}let t=0;while(q.length&&fresh){const nq=[];for(const [r,c] of q)for(const [x,y] of [[r+1,c],[r-1,c],[r,c+1],[r,c-1]])if(x>=0&&y>=0&&x<R&&y<C&&g[x][y]===1){g[x][y]=2;fresh--;nq.push([x,y]);}q=nq;t++;}return fresh?-1:t;}
followups: What if oranges can also be removed over time?

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: A grid heights[r][c] gives the height of each cell. The Pacific Ocean touches the top and left edges; the Atlantic touches the bottom and right edges. Water flows from a cell to a neighbour with equal or lower height. Return all cells [r, c] from which water can reach BOTH oceans, sorted by row and then column.
hint: Going from every cell to the oceans is slow. Reverse it: start from the ocean edges and climb to equal or higher cells.
approach: Run two DFS/BFS passes in reverse. From all Pacific border cells, move to neighbours whose height is >= the current one; mark every cell reached. Do the same from the Atlantic border. The answer is the cells marked by both passes. Each pass visits each cell once, so we avoid the O((mn)^2) cost of starting from every cell.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
solution: function pacificAtlantic(heights){const R=heights.length,C=heights[0].length;const mark=starts=>{const s=Array.from({length:R},()=>new Array(C).fill(false));const st=[...starts];for(const [r,c] of st)s[r][c]=true;while(st.length){const [r,c]=st.pop();for(const [x,y] of [[r+1,c],[r-1,c],[r,c+1],[r,c-1]])if(x>=0&&y>=0&&x<R&&y<C&&!s[x][y]&&heights[x][y]>=heights[r][c]){s[x][y]=true;st.push([x,y]);}}return s;};const pa=[],at=[];for(let r=0;r<R;r++){pa.push([r,0]);at.push([r,C-1]);}for(let c=0;c<C;c++){pa.push([0,c]);at.push([R-1,c]);}const P=mark(pa),A=mark(at),res=[];for(let r=0;r<R;r++)for(let c=0;c<C;c++)if(P[r][c]&&A[r][c])res.push([r,c]);return res;}
followups: Why is the reverse search correct and faster?

title: Word Ladder
statement: Given beginWord, endWord and a list of words, return the number of words in the shortest sequence from beginWord to endWord where each step changes exactly one letter and every new word is in the list. beginWord does not have to be in the list. Return 0 if there is no such sequence.
hint: Words are nodes; two words are connected if they differ by one letter. You want the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
approach: BFS from beginWord. For each word, try replacing each position with each letter a-z; if the new word is in the word set and not yet visited, queue it. The BFS level number plus one is the answer when we reach endWord. BFS finds the fewest steps because every edge has the same cost. Removing a word from the set when visited keeps it linear in the number of candidate words.
complexity: O(N * L * 26) time, O(N * L) space
solution: function ladderLength(beginWord,endWord,wordList){const set=new Set(wordList);if(!set.has(endWord))return 0;let q=[beginWord],steps=1;set.delete(beginWord);while(q.length){const nq=[];for(const w of q){if(w===endWord)return steps;for(let i=0;i<w.length;i++)for(let c=97;c<123;c++){const n=w.slice(0,i)+String.fromCharCode(c)+w.slice(i+1);if(set.has(n)){set.delete(n);nq.push(n);}}}q=nq;steps++;}return 0;}
followups: Bidirectional BFS to speed it up.
Word Ladder II: return all shortest paths.

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are numCourses courses labelled 0 to numCourses-1. Each pair [a, b] in prerequisites means you must take course b before course a. Return true if you can finish all courses (the graph has no cycle).
hint: You can finish iff there is no cycle. Repeatedly take courses with no remaining prerequisites.
approach: Kahn's algorithm: count the in-degree (number of prerequisites) of each course. Queue all courses with in-degree 0. Pop a course, count it as done, and decrease the in-degree of the courses that depend on it, queuing those that reach 0. If all courses get processed, there is no cycle. Courses on a cycle never reach in-degree 0, so they are never processed.
complexity: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
solution: function canFinish(numCourses,prerequisites){const adj=Array.from({length:numCourses},()=>[]),deg=new Array(numCourses).fill(0);for(const [a,b] of prerequisites){adj[b].push(a);deg[a]++;}const q=[];for(let i=0;i<numCourses;i++)if(!deg[i])q.push(i);let done=0;while(q.length){const u=q.pop();done++;for(const v of adj[u])if(--deg[v]===0)q.push(v);}return done===numCourses;}
followups: Detect the cycle with DFS colours instead.

title: Course Schedule II
statement: Same setup as Course Schedule. Return an order in which you can take all courses, or an empty array if it is impossible. A graph can have many valid orders, so to get one answer: always take the available course with the smallest number first.
hint: This is a topological sort. Use a min-heap for the courses that are ready.
approach: Compute in-degrees and put all courses with in-degree 0 in a min-heap. Repeatedly pop the smallest number, append it to the order, and reduce the in-degree of its dependents; push those that reach 0. If the order has fewer than numCourses courses, there is a cycle, so return []. The heap only fixes which valid order we output; the topological logic is the same as Kahn's algorithm.
complexity: O((V + E) log V) time, O(V + E) space
followups: Return all possible topological orders.

title: Alien Dictionary
statement: Words from an alien language are given sorted in that language's dictionary order. Return a string with the letters of the language in a valid order. Return "" if the input is invalid (a cycle, or a longer word placed before its own prefix). When several orders are valid, always pick the alphabetically smallest available letter.
hint: Compare each pair of neighbouring words. The first different letters give one rule "x comes before y". Then topologically sort the letters.
approach: Collect all letters. For each adjacent pair of words, find the first position where they differ and add the edge letter1 -> letter2; if no difference is found and the first word is longer, the input is invalid. Then run Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap on letters. If not all letters get output there is a cycle, so return "". Edges only come from neighbours because sortedness makes the others follow by chain.
complexity: O(C + L log A) time (C total chars, A alphabet size)
followups: How do you detect the "prefix" invalid case?

title: Number of Provinces
statement: There are n cities. isConnected[i][j] = 1 means city i and city j are directly connected (the matrix is symmetric). A province is a group of cities connected directly or indirectly. Return the number of provinces.
hint: Start with every city in its own group. Each connection merges two groups.
approach: Use union-find (disjoint set). Begin with n groups. For each pair (i, j) with a 1, find the roots of i and j; if they differ, merge them and decrease the group count. Path compression makes find almost O(1), so the total is about O(n^2) for scanning the matrix. DFS over the matrix gives the same count.
solution: function findCircleNum(isConnected){const n=isConnected.length,p=Array.from({length:n},(_,i)=>i);const find=x=>{while(p[x]!==x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;};let g=n;for(let i=0;i<n;i++)for(let j=i+1;j<n;j++)if(isConnected[i][j]){const a=find(i),b=find(j);if(a!==b){p[a]=b;g--;}}return g;}
followups: Add union by rank/size. What does it improve?

title: Redundant Connection
statement: A tree with n nodes (labelled 1 to n) had one extra edge added, so it now has n edges and one cycle. Given the edge list, return the edge that can be removed to make it a tree again. If several answers are possible, return the one that appears LAST in the input.
hint: Add edges one by one. When does an edge create a cycle?
approach: Union-find: process edges in order. For edge (u, v), if find(u) == find(v) they are already connected, so this edge closes a cycle; return it. Otherwise merge the two groups. Because we process in order and return the first edge that closes a cycle, the answer is the last edge of that cycle in the input order.
solution: function findRedundantConnection(edges){const p=Array.from({length:edges.length+1},(_,i)=>i);const find=x=>{while(p[x]!==x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;};for(const [u,v] of edges){const a=find(u),b=find(v);if(a===b)return [u,v];p[a]=b;}return [];}
followups: Redundant Connection II for directed graphs.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
statement: Given n nodes labelled 0 to n-1 and a list of undirected edges, return the number of connected components.
hint: Start with n components. Every edge that joins two different components reduces the count by one.
approach: Union-find with a counter set to n. For each edge, find the roots of both ends. If they differ, union them and decrement the counter. At the end the counter is the number of components. Edges inside an already-joined component change nothing, which is why we check the roots first.
complexity: O((n + e) * alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
solution: function countComponents(n,edges){const p=Array.from({length:n},(_,i)=>i);const find=x=>{while(p[x]!==x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;};let c=n;for(const [u,v] of edges){const a=find(u),b=find(v);if(a!==b){p[a]=b;c--;}}return c;}
followups: What if edges arrive as a stream and you must answer after each one?

title: Satisfiability of Equality Equations
statement: You get strings like "a==b" or "a!=b" with single lowercase letters. Return true if it is possible to assign integer values to the letters so that all equations are true.
hint: Equality is transitive, so "==" builds groups. Then check that no "!=" has both letters in the same group.
approach: First pass: for every "==" equation, union the two letters. Second pass: for every "!=" equation, if find(a) == find(b) the equations contradict, so return false. If no contradiction is found, we can give each group its own number. Doing all unions before the checks is important, because order in the input must not matter.
solution: function equationsPossible(equations){const p=Array.from({length:26},(_,i)=>i);const id=c=>c.charCodeAt(0)-97;const find=x=>{while(p[x]!==x){p[x]=p[p[x]];x=p[x];}return x;};for(const e of equations)if(e[1]==='=')p[find(id(e[0]))]=find(id(e[3]));for(const e of equations)if(e[1]==='!'&&find(id(e[0]))===find(id(e[3])))return false;return true;}
followups: Accounts Merge uses the same idea with strings as keys.

title: Network Delay Time
statement: A network has n nodes labelled 1 to n. times is a list of [u, v, w]: a signal from u reaches v in w time units (directed). A signal is sent from node k. Return the time for all nodes to receive it, or -1 if some node never does.
hint: You need the shortest distance from k to every node, then take the largest one. Edge weights are non-negative.
approach: Dijkstra's algorithm with a min-heap of (distance, node). Pop the closest unfinished node; if its distance is stale skip it; otherwise relax each outgoing edge and push improved distances. When the heap is empty, dist[] holds the shortest times. The answer is max(dist), or -1 if some node is unreachable. Greedy choice works because weights are not negative, so the closest node is final when popped.
complexity: O(E log V) time, O(V + E) space
followups: Why does Dijkstra fail with negative edges?

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
statement: There are n cities and flights [from, to, price]. Return the cheapest price from src to dst with at most k stops in between (so at most k + 1 flights), or -1 if no such route exists.
hint: Plain Dijkstra ignores the stop limit. Limit the number of edges: do exactly k + 1 rounds of relaxation.
approach: Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds. Keep dist[] from src. In each round, copy dist to prev, and for every flight (u, v, w) update next[v] = min(next[v], prev[u] + w). Using the copy from the previous round makes sure each round adds exactly one flight, so after round i we know the cheapest route using at most i flights. The answer is dist[dst] after k + 1 rounds.
solution: function findCheapestPrice(n,flights,src,dst,k){let dist=new Array(n).fill(Infinity);dist[src]=0;for(let i=0;i<=k;i++){const nd=[...dist];for(const [u,v,w] of flights)if(dist[u]+w<nd[v])nd[v]=dist[u]+w;dist=nd;}return dist[dst]===Infinity?-1:dist[dst];}
followups: Solve it with a Dijkstra variant whose state is (node, stops used).

title: Path With Minimum Effort
statement: You are given a grid of heights. Move up, down, left or right from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell. The effort of a path is the largest absolute height difference between two neighbouring cells on it. Return the minimum effort over all paths.
hint: It is a shortest-path problem where the "cost" of a path is its maximum edge, not the sum. Dijkstra still works.
approach: Run Dijkstra on the grid cells. The distance of a cell is the smallest possible "max difference so far". When moving to a neighbour, the new cost is max(current cost, |height difference|). Push it if it improves the neighbour. This works because the cost never decreases along a path, which is what Dijkstra needs. The first time we pop the target, we have the answer. Binary search on effort plus BFS is another solution.
complexity: O(m * n * log(m * n)) time, O(m * n) space
followups: Solve it with binary search + BFS and compare.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You are climbing a staircase with n steps. Each time you can climb 1 or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top.
hint: To stand on step n you came from step n-1 or step n-2.
approach: Let ways[i] be the number of ways to reach step i. Then ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2], because the last move was either 1 or 2 steps. With ways[1] = 1 and ways[2] = 2 this is the Fibonacci sequence. We only need the last two values, so two variables are enough.
solution: function climbStairs(n){let a=1,b=1;for(let i=2;i<=n;i++)[a,b]=[b,a+b];return b;}
followups: Allow steps of size 1, 2 or 3.
Compute it in O(log n) with matrix power.

title: House Robber
statement: Houses are in a row and nums[i] is the money in house i. You cannot rob two neighbouring houses. Return the maximum money you can rob.
hint: For each house you either rob it (and skip the previous one) or skip it.
approach: Let best[i] be the maximum money using the first i houses. Then best[i] = max(best[i-1], best[i-2] + nums[i]): skip house i, or rob it and use the best result from two houses back. Only the last two values are needed, so use two variables. The recurrence is correct because the decision at house i only depends on whether house i-1 was robbed, and the formula covers both cases.
solution: function rob(nums){let prev=0,cur=0;for(const x of nums)[prev,cur]=[cur,Math.max(cur,prev+x)];return cur;}
followups: Houses are in a circle (House Robber II).
Also return which houses are robbed.

title: Coin Change
statement: Given coin values and a total amount, return the fewest coins needed to make that amount. You have an unlimited number of each coin. Return -1 if it cannot be made.
hint: Greedy (always take the biggest coin) fails for some coin sets. Build the answer for every amount from 0 up.
approach: Let dp[a] be the fewest coins for amount a, with dp[0] = 0. For each amount a, try every coin c <= a: dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1). If dp[amount] is still infinity, return -1. This works because the best answer for a ends with some coin c, and the rest must be the best answer for a - c (optimal substructure).
solution: function coinChange(coins,amount){const dp=new Array(amount+1).fill(Infinity);dp[0]=0;for(let a=1;a<=amount;a++)for(const c of coins)if(c<=a&&dp[a-c]+1<dp[a])dp[a]=dp[a-c]+1;return dp[amount]===Infinity?-1:dp[amount];}
followups: Count the number of ways to make the amount (Coin Change II).
Why does greedy fail for coins [1,3,4] and amount 6?

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence (elements do not need to be next to each other).
hint: The O(n^2) DP is easy. For O(n log n), keep the smallest possible tail for each subsequence length.
approach: Keep an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest ending value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For each number x, binary search for the first tail >= x and replace it with x; if none exists, append x. tails is always sorted, and its length is the answer. A smaller tail is always better because it is easier to extend later. Note that tails is not itself the subsequence.
complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
solution: function lengthOfLIS(nums){const tails=[];for(const x of nums){let lo=0,hi=tails.length;while(lo<hi){const m=(lo+hi)>>1;if(tails[m]<x)lo=m+1;else hi=m;}tails[lo]=x;}return tails.length;}
followups: Return one actual LIS.
Count the number of LIS.

title: Word Break
statement: Given a string s and a list of words wordDict, return true if s can be split into a sequence of dictionary words (words can be reused).
hint: Let canBreak[i] mean "the first i letters can be split". Which earlier positions j can end a word at i?
approach: dp[0] = true (empty prefix). For each end i from 1 to n, check every start j < i: if dp[j] is true and s[j..i) is in the dictionary, then dp[i] = true. The answer is dp[n]. A word that ends at i is valid only if everything before it can be split, which is exactly dp[j]. Put the words in a set for O(1) lookups.
complexity: O(n^2) set checks (times word length), O(n) space
solution: function wordBreak(s,wordDict){const set=new Set(wordDict),dp=new Array(s.length+1).fill(false);dp[0]=true;for(let i=1;i<=s.length;i++)for(let j=0;j<i;j++)if(dp[j]&&set.has(s.slice(j,i))){dp[i]=true;break;}return dp[s.length];}
followups: Word Break II: return all sentences.

title: Unique Paths
statement: A robot is at the top-left of an m x n grid and can only move right or down. Return the number of different paths to the bottom-right corner.
hint: The number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cell above and the cell on the left.
approach: dp[r][c] = dp[r-1][c] + dp[r][c-1], with the first row and first column equal to 1 (only one way to get there). We only need the previous row, so one array of size n is enough: update dp[c] += dp[c-1] row by row. Math alternative: the answer is C(m+n-2, m-1).
solution: function uniquePaths(m,n){const dp=new Array(n).fill(1);for(let r=1;r<m;r++)for(let c=1;c<n;c++)dp[c]+=dp[c-1];return dp[n-1];}
followups: Add obstacles in the grid (Unique Paths II).

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: Given two strings text1 and text2, return the length of their longest common subsequence (characters in the same order, not necessarily next to each other).
hint: Compare the last characters of the two prefixes. If equal, they can both be part of the answer.
approach: Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length of the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b. If a[i-1] == b[j-1], dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1 (use the matching letter). Otherwise dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]) (drop one letter from either side). The table has (n+1) x (m+1) cells and each is O(1).
complexity: O(n * m) time, O(n * m) space (O(min(n, m)) with rolling rows)
solution: function longestCommonSubsequence(text1,text2){const n=text1.length,m=text2.length;const dp=Array.from({length:n+1},()=>new Array(m+1).fill(0));for(let i=1;i<=n;i++)for(let j=1;j<=m;j++)dp[i][j]=text1[i-1]===text2[j-1]?dp[i-1][j-1]+1:Math.max(dp[i-1][j],dp[i][j-1]);return dp[n][m];}
followups: Print the subsequence itself.
Shortest Common Supersequence.

title: Edit Distance
statement: Given two words word1 and word2, return the minimum number of operations to turn word1 into word2. Allowed operations: insert a letter, delete a letter, replace a letter.
hint: Look at the last letters. If they match, no cost. If not, try the three operations.
approach: dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i letters of word1 and the first j letters of word2. Base cases: dp[i][0] = i (delete all) and dp[0][j] = j (insert all). If the letters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]. Otherwise it is 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] (delete), dp[i][j-1] (insert), dp[i-1][j-1] (replace)). Each cell uses three earlier cells, so filling the table is O(n * m).
complexity: O(n * m) time, O(n * m) space (rolling rows reduce it to O(m))
solution: function minDistance(word1,word2){const n=word1.length,m=word2.length;const dp=Array.from({length:n+1},(_,i)=>{const r=new Array(m+1).fill(0);r[0]=i;return r;});for(let j=0;j<=m;j++)dp[0][j]=j;for(let i=1;i<=n;i++)for(let j=1;j<=m;j++)dp[i][j]=word1[i-1]===word2[j-1]?dp[i-1][j-1]:1+Math.min(dp[i-1][j],dp[i][j-1],dp[i-1][j-1]);return dp[n][m];}
followups: Reduce space to O(min(n, m)).
How would you recover the actual edit steps?

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: Given an array of positive integers nums, return true if it can be split into two subsets with the same sum.
hint: If the total is odd, the answer is no. Otherwise, can some subset reach exactly total / 2? This is 0/1 knapsack.
approach: Let target = sum / 2 (return false if sum is odd). Keep a boolean array can[s] meaning "some subset of the numbers so far sums to s", with can[0] = true. For each number x, update s from target down to x: can[s] = can[s] or can[s - x]. Going downward makes sure each number is used at most once. The answer is can[target].
solution: function canPartition(nums){const sum=nums.reduce((a,b)=>a+b,0);if(sum%2)return false;const t=sum/2,can=new Array(t+1).fill(false);can[0]=true;for(const x of nums)for(let s=t;s>=x;s--)if(can[s-x])can[s]=true;return can[t];}
followups: Why must the inner loop go downward?
Target Sum is the same idea.

title: Maximal Square
statement: Given a binary matrix (an array of strings of "0" and "1"), find the largest square containing only 1s and return its area.
hint: Let dp[r][c] be the side of the largest all-1 square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c). It depends on three neighbours.
approach: If the cell is "1", dp[r][c] = 1 + min(dp[r-1][c], dp[r][c-1], dp[r-1][c-1]); otherwise 0. The smallest of the three neighbours limits how far the square can grow, because all three must be full squares. The answer is the largest dp value squared. We touch each cell once.
complexity: O(m * n) time, O(n) space with a rolling row
solution: function maximalSquare(matrix){let best=0;const R=matrix.length,C=R?matrix[0].length:0;const dp=Array.from({length:R+1},()=>new Array(C+1).fill(0));for(let r=1;r<=R;r++)for(let c=1;c<=C;c++)if(matrix[r-1][c-1]==='1'){dp[r][c]=1+Math.min(dp[r-1][c],dp[r][c-1],dp[r-1][c-1]);best=Math.max(best,dp[r][c]);}return best*best;}
followups: Maximal Rectangle: how is it related to histograms?

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement: Implement a Trie with insert(word), search(word) (true if the exact word was inserted) and startsWith(prefix) (true if any inserted word starts with it). Input: a list of operations and a list of argument lists. Return a list of results: null for the constructor and insert, a boolean for search and startsWith.
hint: Each node keeps a map from a letter to a child node and a flag that says "a word ends here".
approach: A trie stores words letter by letter along a path from the root. insert walks/creates the nodes for each letter and marks the last node as an end. search walks the letters and checks the end flag; startsWith only checks that the path exists. Every operation costs O(L) for a word of length L, independent of how many words are stored, and words that share a prefix share nodes.
complexity: O(L) per operation, O(total letters) space
solution: function runTrie(ops,args){const root={ch:{},end:false};const walk=w=>{let n=root;for(const c of w){if(!n.ch[c])return null;n=n.ch[c];}return n;};return ops.map((op,i)=>{const w=args[i][0];if(op==='insert'){let n=root;for(const c of w){if(!n.ch[c])n.ch[c]={ch:{},end:false};n=n.ch[c];}n.end=true;return null;}if(op==='search'){const n=walk(w);return !!(n&&n.end);}if(op==='startsWith')return walk(w)!==null;return null;});}
followups: Add delete(word).
Return the number of words with a given prefix.

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
statement: Design a WordDictionary with addWord(word) and search(word), where search may contain "." that matches any one letter. Input: a list of operations and a list of argument lists. Return null for the constructor and addWord, and a boolean for search.
hint: Use a trie. When you meet ".", try all children.
approach: Store words in a trie. For search, run a DFS over the pattern: for a letter, follow that child; for ".", try every child and return true if any path works. A path succeeds when the pattern is finished and the node is marked as a word end. Without dots the search is O(L); each dot can branch up to 26 times in the worst case.
complexity: addWord O(L); search O(L) with no dots, up to O(26^d * L) with d dots
solution: function runWordDictionary(ops,args){const root={ch:{},end:false};const find=(n,w,i)=>{if(i===w.length)return n.end;if(w[i]==='.'){for(const k in n.ch)if(find(n.ch[k],w,i+1))return true;return false;}return n.ch[w[i]]?find(n.ch[w[i]],w,i+1):false;};return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op==='addWord'){let n=root;for(const c of args[i][0]){if(!n.ch[c])n.ch[c]={ch:{},end:false};n=n.ch[c];}n.end=true;return null;}if(op==='search')return find(root,args[i][0],0);return null;});}
followups: Support "*" that matches any sequence of letters.

title: Word Search II
statement: Given a grid of letters (array of strings) and a list of words, return all words from the list that can be built from adjacent cells (up, down, left, right) without reusing a cell inside one word. Return them in any order.
hint: Running Word Search once per word is slow. Put all words in a trie and search the grid once.
approach: Build a trie of all words. DFS from every cell, walking down the trie together with the grid: if the next letter has no trie child, stop immediately (pruning). When a node marks a word end, add that word to the results and clear the mark so it is not added twice. Mark cells as visited while going deeper and restore them when backtracking. One DFS serves all words at once.
complexity: O(m * n * 3^L) worst case, but pruned heavily by the trie; O(total word letters) space
solution: function findWords(board,words){const root={};for(const w of words){let n=root;for(const c of w)n=n[c]=n[c]||{};n.$=w;}const g=board.map(r=>r.split('')),R=g.length,C=g[0].length,res=[];const go=(r,c,node)=>{const ch=g[r][c],nx=node[ch];if(!nx)return;if(nx.$){res.push(nx.$);nx.$=null;}g[r][c]='#';for(const [x,y] of [[r+1,c],[r-1,c],[r,c+1],[r,c-1]])if(x>=0&&y>=0&&x<R&&y<C&&g[x][y]!=='#')go(x,y,nx);g[r][c]=ch;};for(let r=0;r<R;r++)for(let c=0;c<C;c++)go(r,c,root);return res;}
followups: Why is it useful to remove trie nodes that are no longer needed?

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: Given a string s, return its longest palindromic substring. If several have the same length, return the leftmost one. For an empty string return an empty string.
hint: Every palindrome has a center. Expand outward from each possible center.
approach: There are 2n - 1 centers (n letters and n - 1 gaps between letters). For each center, expand left and right while the two letters are equal, and remember the longest result. Going over centers from left to right with a strict "longer than" check keeps the leftmost on ties. It is O(n^2) in the worst case but uses O(1) space; Manacher's algorithm makes it O(n).
solution: function longestPalindrome(s){let bs=0,bl=0;for(let c=0;c<2*s.length-1;c++){let l=c>>1,r=l+(c&1);while(l>=0&&r<s.length&&s[l]===s[r]){l--;r++;}if(r-l-1>bl){bl=r-l-1;bs=l+1;}}return s.substr(bs,bl);}
followups: Count all palindromic substrings.
Solve it in O(n) with Manacher's algorithm.

title: Longest Common Prefix
statement: Given an array of strings, return the longest common prefix of all of them, or an empty string if there is none.
hint: The prefix cannot be longer than the shortest word. Compare column by column.
approach: Take the first word as a reference. For each position i, check that every other word has the same letter at i. At the first mismatch (or when a word ends) return the prefix found so far. We look at each letter at most once, so the cost is the total number of letters. A trie would also work, but it is more than needed here.
solution: function longestCommonPrefix(strs){if(!strs.length)return '';for(let i=0;i<strs[0].length;i++)for(const w of strs)if(i>=w.length||w[i]!==strs[0][i])return strs[0].slice(0,i);return strs[0];}
followups: Find the longest common prefix of many strings queried repeatedly.

title: Single Number
statement: Every number in the array appears twice, except one that appears once. Return that single number. Use O(1) extra space and O(n) time.
hint: What is a ^ a? What is a ^ 0? Does the order of XOR matter?
approach: XOR has three useful rules: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x, and it is commutative and associative. XOR all numbers together: every pair cancels to 0 and only the single number is left. This is O(n) time with one integer of memory, better than a hash set.
solution: function singleNumber(nums){let x=0;for(const n of nums)x^=n;return x;}
followups: Two numbers appear once, all others twice (Single Number III).

title: Number of 1 Bits
statement: Given a non-negative integer n (up to 32 bits), return the number of bits that are 1 in its binary form (the Hamming weight).
hint: n & (n - 1) removes the lowest set bit. How many times can you do that?
approach: Each time we compute n = n & (n - 1), the lowest 1 bit becomes 0 (subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 and all zeros below it, and the AND clears them). Count how many steps it takes to reach 0. The loop runs once per set bit, so at most 32 times. Use unsigned shifts (n >>> 0) in JavaScript to avoid sign problems.
complexity: O(k) time where k = number of set bits, O(1) space
solution: function hammingWeight(n){n=n>>>0;let c=0;while(n){n=(n&(n-1))>>>0;c++;}return c;}
followups: Count bits for every number from 0 to n (Counting Bits) using DP.

title: Sum of Two Integers
statement: Return the sum of two integers a and b without using the + or - operators (use bit operations).
hint: XOR adds without carry. AND shifted left by one gives the carry.
approach: Adding two bits: sum without carry is a ^ b, and the carry is (a & b) << 1. Add them again the same way, repeating until the carry is 0. Each round pushes the carry at least one bit to the left, so it ends within 32 rounds. JavaScript bit operations use 32-bit signed integers, which gives the right two's complement behaviour for negative numbers.
complexity: O(1) time (at most 32 rounds), O(1) space
solution: function getSum(a,b){while(b!==0){const carry=(a&b)<<1;a=a^b;b=carry;}return a;}
followups: Subtract two numbers without the - operator.

title: Single Number II
statement: Every number appears exactly three times, except one that appears once. Return the single number in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
hint: Count how many numbers have each bit set. For each bit, the count modulo 3 tells you the bit of the answer.
approach: For each of the 32 bit positions, add up the bits of all numbers. Numbers that appear three times contribute a multiple of 3, so the remainder (count % 3) is the bit of the single number. Rebuild the result from these bits; use |0 to get a signed 32-bit value. There is also a constant-state trick with two variables (ones, twos) that act as a 2-bit counter for every bit position at once.
solution: function singleNumberII(nums){let r=0;for(let b=0;b<32;b++){let c=0;for(const n of nums)c+=(n>>b)&1;if(c%3)r|=(1<<b);}return r|0;}
followups: Same problem if every other number appears 5 times.

title: LRU Cache
statement: Design an LRU (least recently used) cache with a fixed capacity. LRUCache(capacity), get(key) returns the value or -1, and put(key, value) inserts or updates a key; when the cache is full, it first removes the least recently used key. Both get and put count as a "use". Input: a list of operation names and a list of argument lists. Return a list: null for the constructor and put, the value for get.
hint: You need O(1) lookup and O(1) "move to most recent" and "remove oldest". A hash map plus a doubly linked list does this. In JavaScript, a Map remembers insertion order.
approach: Hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordered by recency (head = most recent, tail = least recent). get: find the node, move it to the head, return the value. put: if the key exists, update and move to the head; otherwise add at the head and, if size > capacity, remove the tail and its map entry. All steps are pointer changes, so O(1). In JavaScript, you can use a Map: delete the key and set it again to make it newest, and the first key of the Map is the oldest.
solution: function runLRUCache(ops,args){let cap=0;const m=new Map();return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op==='LRUCache'){cap=args[i][0];return null;}if(op==='get'){const k=args[i][0];if(!m.has(k))return -1;const v=m.get(k);m.delete(k);m.set(k,v);return v;}const [k,v]=args[i];m.delete(k);m.set(k,v);if(m.size>cap)m.delete(m.keys().next().value);return null;});}
followups: Implement it with your own doubly linked list.
LFU Cache: evict the least frequently used key.
How would you make it thread-safe?

title: Logger Rate Limiter
statement: Design a logger that prints each distinct message at most once every 10 seconds. shouldPrintMessage(timestamp, message) returns true if the message may be printed now, else false. A message printed at time t blocks the same message until time t + 10 (it is allowed again at t + 10). Timestamps never go backwards. Input: operation names and argument lists. Return null for the constructor and a boolean for each call.
hint: Remember when each message was last printed. Only update that time when you actually allow it.
approach: Keep a hash map from message to the next allowed timestamp. On a call, if the message is not in the map or timestamp >= its stored value, allow it and set the stored value to timestamp + 10. Otherwise reject without changing the map. This is a per-key fixed cooldown, the simplest form of rate limiting. The map can grow forever, so a real service would also expire old entries.
complexity: O(1) per call, O(distinct messages) space
solution: function runLogger(ops,args){const next=new Map();return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op!=='shouldPrintMessage')return null;const [t,msg]=args[i];if(next.has(msg)&&t<next.get(msg))return false;next.set(msg,t+10);return true;});}

title: Design Hit Counter
statement: Design a HitCounter that counts hits in the past 300 seconds (a hit at time t is counted for times t+1 up to t+299, that is, a hit is counted at time T if T - 300 < t <= T). hit(timestamp) records a hit; getHits(timestamp) returns the number of hits in the past 300 seconds. Timestamps are non-decreasing. Input: operation names and argument lists. Return null for the constructor and hit, and the count for getHits.
hint: Hits come in time order, so old hits are always at the front. Use a queue and drop expired hits.
approach: This is a sliding-window log, the same idea as a sliding-window rate limiter. Keep a queue of hit timestamps. On getHits(T), pop from the front while the timestamp <= T - 300; the queue size is the answer. Each hit is pushed once and popped once, so the amortized cost is O(1). If one second can have millions of hits, store (second, count) pairs, or a circular array of 300 buckets, to bound the memory.
complexity: O(1) amortized per operation, O(hits in window) space
solution: function runHitCounter(ops,args){const q=[];let head=0;return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op==='hit'){q.push(args[i][0]);return null;}if(op==='getHits'){const T=args[i][0];while(head<q.length&&q[head]<=T-300)head++;return q.length-head;}return null;});}
followups: Hits per second can be huge: how do you save memory?
Hits arrive out of order.
Make it a per-user rate limiter that allows at most N requests per window.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
statement: Design a store where set(key, value, timestamp) saves a value, and get(key, timestamp) returns the value saved with the largest timestamp <= the given timestamp, or "" if there is none. Timestamps for each key are given in increasing order. Input: operation names and argument lists. Return null for the constructor and set, and the string for get.
hint: For each key keep a list of (timestamp, value) in sorted order. Which search finds the "largest timestamp <= t"?
approach: A hash map from key to an array of [timestamp, value] pairs. Because timestamps for a key only increase, each array is already sorted, so set is just an append. For get, binary search the array for the last pair whose timestamp is <= the query; return its value, or "" if none. Binary search turns a linear scan into O(log n).
complexity: set O(1), get O(log n), O(total entries) space
solution: function runTimeMap(ops,args){const m=new Map();return ops.map((op,i)=>{if(op==='set'){const [k,v,t]=args[i];if(!m.has(k))m.set(k,[]);m.get(k).push([t,v]);return null;}if(op==='get'){const [k,t]=args[i];const a=m.get(k)||[];let lo=0,hi=a.length;while(lo<hi){const mid=(lo+hi)>>1;if(a[mid][0]<=t)lo=mid+1;else hi=mid;}return lo?a[lo-1][1]:'';}return null;});}
followups: What if timestamps for a key can arrive out of order?
